title: Playing in Alabama, Selma and visiting Montgomery
summary: Sal describes working the Dixie Club near an air base, and a trip to Montgomery.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, I didn't travel much. I just played around Louisiana here. A few times, I'd sit like Corksdale. And Alabama, you played? Alabama, I played in Tuscaloosa, Basma, what the hell the name of that plays? Well, integration thing, huh? Selma. Selma. Oh man, I played that. The man said, honey, well, I played with David Lewis Escobeda. Do you know Escobeda? No, I don't know him. Yeah, but.
I've heard of him, but I don't know him.

He's a fine musician. He plays trumpet, vibes, and piano all over the band. We had a broad saying, I see, stupid, who you met at? You remember the night I was talking to Danny Dean, and the broad said, hello, Sal, Gloria, Gloria. We had Gloria, I see. And we were lying to it, but all the mines, Mississippi, no mines, Mississippi, no hills, no hills, no hills, no hills. Oh, this is beautiful, Mississippi, man. We were going up to Selma, you know, and I called. Four guys in this broad, you see. She was the second in the band. So we got to the place, the Dixie Club. The guy said, wow, they're going to paint this band, man. The guy had to cover the pigs to pay up, man. I asked for the guy making mistakes, see. They had a big air base there, a great air base, you know, and people from all over, man. Right across the creek, you could drink, you could raise hell, see. We used to pack them in over there, see. So one day, I told the owner, I said, like, we're off on a Monday, see. I like to take a trip to Montgomery, man. He says, you know nobody up there? I said, yeah, the police commissioner up there, said, Clyde Sellers. You know him? I said, yes, my brother knows. He said, man, Clyde, I have a good body, man. I take it right to his house, big car like that. We drove up there, hey, and I used to be in the car with me, see. That's the mistake people make, see. When they go to a small town, they think about the stupid ass, it's really wrong. I said, I'm going to show him in the van, but a whole beat up car like me, you know. We drove up there, big, West Street, Montgomery, man. West Paris Street, big column, that man, where the governor's house. You sure you're right, man? I said, sure, I'm right. We drove up there, he went out in the law, man. All those sounds, he said, come on in. He looked at that pub, and that's the place. He says, where's Clyde? I said, be back shortly. Up in town, man.
